text: quod, ὃ in quibusdam mss. sumpsisse pro conjunctione, ideoque posuisse quia : quemadmodum interpres Græcus epistolæ 5 Martini Papæ I, ad Joannem Philadelphiæ episcopum, quod manifestatum est in carne, vertit ὡς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκί. Nisi quis velit, quod non puto, scriptum fuisse a Liberato : Qui apparuit in carne, justificatus est in spiritu. Juxta illud Eucherii, epistola de contemptu mundi, n. 54 : Itaque manifestatus est in carne, justificatus est spiritu, apparuit angelis, prædicatus est gentibus, creditus est in mundo, assumptus est in gloria. Secundo ex sequentibus colligo quædam exemplaria tempore Anastasii et Macedonii habuisse ὃς θεός, ut mutatione facta ὃς in ὡς intelligeretur ὡς θεός, ut esset Deus. Subit denique admirari, cum manifesta sit calumnia in Macedonium, tamen Fulbertum rem pro veritate accepisse, epist. 1 : Et illum Apostoli locum ubi dicit : « Quod apparuit in carne vivificatum (pro justificatum) est in spiritu. » Quem (f. Ad quem) locum Macedonius per immutationem Scripturæ apostolicum dictum sic voluit definire, idest, ut esset Deus, apparuit in carne ; necnon illo vetustiorem Hincmarum, opusculo 33, cap. 18 et 22. Hincmari varians lectio mirifica est. Quidam, inquit priori loco, ipsas Scripturas verbis illicitis imposturaverunt ; sicut Macedonius Constantinopolitanus episcopus, qui ab Anastasio imperatore ideo a civitate expulsus legitur, quoniam falsavit Evangelia, et illum Apostolis locum ubi dicit : « Quod apparuit in carne, justificatum est in spiritu, » per cognationem Græcarum litterarum Ο et Θ hoc modo mutando falsavit. Ubi enim  habuit qui, hoc est ΟΣ, monosyllabum Græcum, littera mutata Ο in Θ vertit et fecit ΘΣ id est, ut esset Deus apparuit per carnem. Quapropter tanquam Nestorianus fuit expulsus. Qua de varietate sic sentio, vel Hincmarum vel ipsius exscriptorem mala fide hic egisse, atque in Θ et ΘΣ mutasse Ω et ΩΣ. Suum tamen et unicuique esto judicium.
en: Note continuing from the previous page (its marker and opening are not on this page). It argues that 1 Tim 3:16 was read in some manuscripts, in the time of Anastasius and Macedonius, as 'hos theos' (ὃς θεός), so that by changing ὃς to ὡς it would be understood 'as God, that he might be God'. It cites the Greek translator of Pope Martin I's 5th letter to John of Philadelphia, Liberatus, Eucherius (letter on contempt of the world, n. 54), Fulbert (epist. 1) and Hincmar (opusc. 33, chs. 18 and 22). The editor finds it wonderful that Hincmar says Macedonius, expelled by Emperor Anastasius, falsified the Gospels by changing Ο to Θ, so that ΟΣ became ΘΣ, 'that he might be God, he appeared through the flesh', and so was expelled as a Nestorian. The editor thinks Hincmar or his copyist acted in bad faith, having changed Ω and ΩΣ into Θ and ΘΣ; let each form his own judgment.

text: Κώδικα. In usu præcipue sunt κῶδιξ, κωδίκιον, κωδίκελλος, κωδικέλλιον. Rarius invenies κωδίκους et κωδικέλους, quorum primum occurrit in Triade martyrum Combefisiana, p. 18 ; posterius homil. Macarii 29 ; Anonymus in Demonstrationibus Chronicis seu Antiquitatibus CP. οἱ Κωδικέλλιοι. f. Κωδικέλλιοι, qui a codicillis. Martyrium Theodori militum præfecti, scriptum a Varo, apud Allatium, De Symeonum scriptis, p. 113 : Οὔαρος Νοτάριος καὶ Ἀποκωδικέλλων.
anchorLine: δικος (y), καὶ ἀναγνοὺς τοῦ βασιλέως τὸ ὄνομα, εἴ-
en: Kodika (codex). In common use are kodix, kodikion, kodikellos, kodikellion. Rarer are kodikous and kodikelous, of which the first occurs in the Combefis Triad of martyrs, p. 18, the second in Macarius hom. 29; the Anonymus in the Chronicle Demonstrations or Antiquities of Constantinople has 'the Kodikellioi', perhaps to be read 'Kodikellioi, those from codicils'. The martyrdom of Theodore, prefect of soldiers, written by Varus, in Allatius, De Symeonum scriptis, p. 113, has: Varus Notarius and Apokodikellon.

text: Ἀστραπῆς. Isidorus, lib. III. Originum, cap. ult. Scorpium quoque et sagittarium propter fulgura mensis ipsius appellaverunt. Sagittarius vir equinis cruribus deformatur, cui sagittam et arcum adjungunt, ut ex eo mensis ipsius fulmina demonstrentur. Unde et sagittarius est vocatus. Quæ ideo protuli, ut per ea tollerem mendum forte typographicum e Rabano libro De computo, cap. 59. t. I Miscellaneorum Baluzianorum : Scorpium et Sagittarium equinis cruribus deformatum, propter flumina (fulmina) mensium ipsorum, October et November accipiunt. Huc etiam pertinere potest locus turpissimo mendo deformatus, epist. 38 Theophylacti, ἵνα ταύτῃ καὶ τῷ διεγγίζοις, καὶ τοῦ κεραυνοῦ τηροῖο ἀπείρατος ex interprete : Ut hoc pacto ad illud saltem propius accedas, et ab ingenti fulmine, te illius penitus inexpertem tuteris. Atque ita emaculandus τῷ Διὶ ἐγγίζοις. Ex vulgari adagio, πόρρω Διός τε καὶ κεραυνοῦ. De quo Parœmiographi, et Synesius, De regno, p. 11, ex cujus textu Suidas et Michael Apostolus corrigi debent.
anchorLine: Καὶ μετὰ δύο ἡμέρας, ἀστραπῆς (z) γενομένης με-
en: Astrapes (lightning). Isidore, Origines III, last chapter: they called Scorpio and Sagittarius after the lightnings of that month; Sagittarius is a man with horse's legs, given a bow and arrow so that the month's lightnings may be indicated. The editor cites these to remove a probable printer's error in Rabanus, De computo ch. 59 (Baluze, Miscellanea I): 'flumina' should be 'fulmina'. The same may apply to a badly corrupt passage in Theophylact, epist. 38: it should be emended to 'τῷ Διὶ ἐγγίζοις' ('you would approach Zeus'), from the common saying 'far from Zeus and the thunderbolt', treated by the paroemiographers and by Synesius, De regno, p. 11, from whose text Suidas and Michael Apostolus ought to be corrected.

text: Βροντῆς. Præstat consulere antiquos, quam recentioribus licet doctissimis credere. Itaque ex Apollodoro lib. 1 Bibliothecæ, et Tzetze, chiliade 7, vers. 91, erunt Salmonei tonitrua ἐκ βύρσης, non ἐκ κύρσης, in Vita Nicephori CP. ab Ignatio diacono scripta, n. 81, ad Martii 13 ; Hesychius, βυρσατόνος, τύμπανον ; vel ex alt. edit. βύρσας, τόνος, τύμπανον. Phavorinus, βυρσάτονος, τοῦ τυμπάνου. Castigandum opinor, βύρσα, τόνος τυμπάνου.
anchorLine: γάλης καὶ βροντῆς (a), πάνυ θροηθεὶς ἀπέδωκεν τὸ
en: Brontes (thunder). It is better to consult the ancients than to trust even very learned moderns. So from Apollodorus, Bibliotheca I, and Tzetzes, Chiliad 7, v. 91, Salmoneus's thunders will be 'from a hide' (ἐκ βύρσης), not 'ἐκ κύρσης', as in the Life of Nicephorus of CP by Ignatius the deacon, n. 81, at 13 March; Hesychius has 'byrsatonos, a drum'; or in another edition 'byrsas, tonos, drum'; Phavorinus 'byrsatonos, of the drum'. The editor thinks it should be corrected to 'byrsa, tonos tympanou' (hide, tone of a drum).

anchorLine: καὶ σαγίου καὶ μεγαλείου (c), καὶ καυκίου ²⁸ ξυλίνου.

text: Μεγαλείου, et cap. 87, μεγαλεῖον ἔχον ἀργυροῦν σταυρόν, exponi debet de codice sacræ Scripturæ, qui merito per ἀντονομασίαν et excellentiam magnale vocetur, magnale Dei, divina magnalia continens atque enarrans. Juris Græco-Romani, p. 120, de Judæorum jurejurando, κρατήσῃ ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτοῦ τὸ μεγαλεῖον. Et Cyrillus Scythopolitanus in Vita S. Sabæ. cap. 32 : Παρεγγυήσας αὐτοῖς τὸ μεγαλεῖον καὶ τὴν λοιπὴν ἀκολουθίαν ἐν ταῖς συνάξεσιν Ἀρμενιστὶ καθ' ἑαυτοὺς λέγειν.
anchorLine: καὶ σαγίου καὶ μεγαλείου (c), καὶ καυκίου ²⁸ ξυλίνου.
en: Megaleion (also in ch. 87, "a megaleion having a silver cross") should be understood of a codex of Sacred Scripture, which is rightly called by antonomasia and excellence the magnale, the magnale of God, containing and recounting the divine magnalia. Compare Juris Graeco-Romani, p. 120, on the oath of the Jews: "he shall hold the megaleion in his hands"; and Cyril of Scythopolis, Life of St Sabas, ch. 32: "having charged them to say the megaleion and the rest of the service in Armenian by themselves in their assemblies".

text: Τάγμα. Psellus, Dialogo de operatione dæmonum, p. 18 : τοῖς ἀντικειμένοις πράγμασιν. Ex Gaulmino, πνεύμασιν, per me τάγμασιν.
anchorLine: εἰς τὸ τάγμα (d) τῆς Δεσποίνης
en: Tagma (order, rank). Psellus, Dialogue on the Operation of Demons, p. 18, has 'τοῖς ἀντικειμένοις πράγμασιν'. From Gaulmin, 'πνεύμασιν'; in my view, 'τάγμασιν'.

text: Σκαμνίον, σκάμνος, σκάμνον, σκαμνεῖον. Unde σκαμνάλια, et forte σκαμνάριος, in Prochori Historia, ubi vulgo, Σκαμβάριος δέ τις ὀνόματι Σέλευκος. Apud Hilarium veteres editiones scamnellum et scamnello pro scabellum et scabello. In psal. cxviii, 91.
anchorLine: εἰς σκαμνίον (e), ἡ εἰς τὰ βαθμίδια τοῦ ἱερατείου τὰ φολερά (f)
en: Skamnion, skamnos, skamnon, skamneion (a stool). Hence skamnalia, and perhaps skamnarios, in the History of Prochorus, where the vulgate has 'a certain Skambarios by name Seleucus'. In Hilary the old editions have scamnellum and scamnello for scabellum and scabello. In Psalm 118:91.

text: Τὰ φολερά. Et cap. iii, hic, φόλεις, φολερά. Usitatum φόλεις. Rarum φολερά. Unde fuit depravatum, cap. 83 Joannis nostri, ἀπὸ φαλερῶν ε'. Quod non intelligens Ambrosius Camaldulensis interpres, nec valens emendare, penitus omisit. In Chronico Marcellini, Nummis, quos Romani Terentianos vel Teruncianos vocant, Græci follares, aut follerales. Anastasius princeps suo nomine figuralis, placibilem plebi commutationem distraxit.
anchorLine: τὰ φολερά (f)
en: Ta folera. Also ch. 3 here: folleis, folera. Folleis is the usual form, folera the rare one. Hence it was corrupted in ch. 83 of our John to 'apo phaleron 5'. Ambrose of Camaldoli, the translator, not understanding it and unable to emend it, omitted it entirely. In the Chronicle of Marcellinus: coins which the Romans call Terentiani or Teruncianii, the Greeks follares or follerales. The emperor Anastasius, under his own name, devised a figured coin changing it to one pleasing to the people.

text: Σιωπήσας τὸ σύνολον. A Meursio editus Eusebius, in Canticum canticorum, p. 42 : Ἀποδεκτικὴ δέ ἐστιν σιωπὴ, ἐν τῷ ἐπιστημόνως κρύπτοντι, καὶ τῷ μισουμένῳ τὰ θειότερα, καὶ μείζω τῆς τῶν ἀκροατῶν δυνάμεως. Non dubito quin scribendum sit, ἀποδεκτή, et μυουμένῳ vel μυομένῳ et ἀκροατῶν. Id est : Laudandum porro est silentium, in eo qui perite celat, quique diviniora et auditorum vires superantia edoctus est, aut occultat.
anchorLine: δύο ἡμέρας νηστεύων, καὶ σιωπήσας (g) τὸ σύνολον, μήτε λαλήσας πρός τινα.
en: Having kept silence altogether. Eusebius, On the Song of Songs, edited by Meursius, p. 42: "Silence is acceptable in one who conceals knowledgeably, and to one who hates the diviner things, and what is greater than the power of the hearers." I do not doubt that one should write apodekte (acceptable), and myoumeno or myomeno (initiated), and akroaton (hearers). That is: silence is to be praised in one who conceals skilfully, who has been taught things too divine and beyond the hearers' strength, or hides them.

anchorLine: λον Θεοῦ, ἔχοντα τὸ μοναστήριον αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸν ³¹

text: Κουσούλλιον. Et cap. 131, infra, κουσσούλιν (quod vertitur casulam, cap. 63, lib. iv Vitæ Gregorii ; sicut in eadem Vita, lib. ii, cap. 45. καμίσιον). Tomo autem I istorum Monumentorum, p. 491, C. κουσσούλιον, vestis genus. In Lexico cod. Reg. 2602, κάμασος καὶ κάμασον, τὸ πικότζουλον. Psellus De grammatica, κάμασον, τὸ πικούτζουλον, pro ἐπικούτζουλον ex Meursio. Τὰ πτερύγια τῶν κουτζούλων, vel κοτζύλων, apud Georgium Alexandrinum in Vita Chrysostomi, n. 42, p. 217. l. xxii. Nec plura invenire potui circa hanc vocem. Deducitur forte aut a κουτζός, mutilus, decurtatus, aut a cosue e cusire, cusuere, consuere, coudre.
anchorLine: καὶ ἀπέδυσαν αὐτὸν τὸ κουσούλλιον (h) (p-0073/0074 top right; line not verified at 600 dpi)
en: Kousoullion. Also ch. 131, below, 'koussoulin' (rendered 'casula' in ch. 63, bk. 4 of the Life of Gregory; as in the same Life, bk. 2, ch. 45, 'kamision'). In vol. 1 of these Monumenta, p. 491, C: koussoulion, a kind of garment. In the Lexicon of Royal MS 2602: kamasos and kamason, the pikotzoulon. Psellus, De grammatica, kamason, pikoutzoulon, for epikoutzoulon, from Meursius. 'The wings of the koutzoula, or kotzyla' in George of Alexandria, Life of Chrysostom, n. 42, p. 217, l. 22. The editor could find no more on this word. It is perhaps derived from koutzos (mutilated, docked), or from the French cosue/cusire, Latin cusuere, consuere, coudre (to sew).

text: Εἰδέας. Cyrillus, in Malachiam, n. 23 Τῆς ἀρετῆς τὸ κάλλος ἐκφανεστέραν ἔχει τὴν εἰδέαν, εἰ δὴ παρακέοιτό τις φαυλότης, ἡ ἁμαρτία. Virtutis elegantia, si qua nequitia, aut peccatum fuerit e regione collatum, splendidior apparet. Est ergo typographicum erratum ἔνδειαν.
en: Eideas (forms/appearance). Cyril, On Malachi, n. 23: 'The beauty of virtue has a more conspicuous appearance if some baseness or sin is set beside it.' The elegance of virtue, if any wickedness or sin is set opposite, appears more splendid. So 'endeian' is a printer's error.

text: Χρηματίσωμεν. Sancti Cyrilli præclare contra Catharos disserentis Comment. in Malachiam, n. 58, verba ut clara sint atque etiam sana, ad hunc
anchorLine: ὅπως ναοὶ Θεοῦ χρηματίσωμεν (j).
en: Chrematisomen (we may be styled). Of St Cyril, excellently disputing against the Cathari, Commentary on Malachi, n. 58: that his words may be clear and sound, to this ... (the note breaks off at the foot of the page, to continue on the next page).

text: fere modum constituantur et legantur : Ὅθεν ἰδεῖν ἔστιν, ὡς δεινήν τινα τῷ βίῳ τὴν νόσον εἰσφέρουσι οἱ τὴν τῆς μετανοίας κιβδηλεύοντες χάριν, καὶ σφίσιν αὐτοῖς ἐπιφημίζοντες οὐχ ἀληθῶς τὸ τῆς καθαρότητος ὄνομα· καίτοι πῶς οὐκ ἄμεινον ἐννοεῖν, ὅτι τὸ οἴεσθαι τε καὶ χρηματισθῆναι καθαροὺς, ἀκαθαρσίας αὖθις τῆς ἐσχάτης ἐπίκλημα φέρει; Hoc est : Unde cernere est, illos gravem in vitam morbum inrehere, qui pœnitentiæ gratiam adulterant, et sibi ipsis falso puritatis nomen ascribunt : quanquam quo modo non erat melius cogitare, quod putare se et vocare puros, crimen illis infert extremæ impuritatis? Δεινὴν posui pro δεινά· οὐκ ἀληθῶς pro ἀληθῶς, et χρηματισθῆναι pro χρηναι, ut et cap. 9, lib. i in Joannem, t. IV, p. 103 B ; supplendum conjicio χρηματισθέντες, ubi habetur υἱοὶ δὲ οἱ χρι..... τοῦ Θεοῦ, quod et sequentia ostendunt.
anchorLine: (continuation of note (j) from p-0074; anchored at 'χρηματίσωμεν (j)' there)
en: (Continuing note j, Cyril against the Cathari:) '...are set and read almost in this way: Hence one may see that those who counterfeit the grace of repentance and falsely give themselves the name of purity bring a dire sickness into life. Yet would it not be better to reflect that to suppose oneself and be styled pure brings in turn the charge of extreme impurity?' That is: from this one can see that those who adulterate the grace of repentance and ascribe to themselves falsely the name of purity bring a grave disease into life; although how was it not better to consider that thinking oneself and being called pure imputes extreme impurity? The editor puts 'deinen' for 'deina', 'ouk alethos' for 'alethos', and 'chrematisthenai' for 'chrenai', as in ch. 9, bk. 1, on John, vol. 4, p. 103 B; he conjectures 'chrematisthentes' should be supplied, where it reads 'sons of the ... of God', as what follows also shows.

text: Ἡ τυχοῦσα. Ineple apud Dorotheum, doctrina 13, ediderunt : Οὐ παραβλέπει ὁ Θεὸς, ὁ οὕτως ἐλεήμων, οὐδὲ τὴν ψυχοῦσαν ἡμῶν θλῖψιν · pro τυχοῦσαν· Non despicit Deus, qui ita misericors est, neque mediocrem afflictionem nostram.
anchorLine: Οὐ γὰρ τυχοῦσα (k) ἡμῖν γίνεται τιμὴ ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι αἰῶνι (l).
en: Hei tychousa (the ordinary/common one). Foolishly, in Dorotheus, doctrine 13, they printed: 'God does not overlook, he who is so merciful, nor our psychousan (cooling) affliction'; for tychousan. [That is:] God does not despise, being so merciful, even a moderate affliction of ours.

text: Ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι αἰῶνι. Chrysostomus in Comparatione regis et monachi, paulo ante finem : Περὶ μὲν οὖν τῶν ἐν τῷ παρόντι βίῳ πραγμάτων ἱκανῶς εἰρῆσθαί μοι δοκεῖ. Εἰ δὲ καὶ τὸν ἀγῶνα τὸν μέλλοντα βουληθείημεν ἐξετάζειν. Videtur legendum αἰῶνα. Idem, seu quis alius, in principium indictionis t. V, Savil. p. 815, l. xxiii : Οὐ προσκυνοῦμεν ἀγῶνα τὸν εἰς φθορὰν ἡμᾶς ἕλκοντα. Volo pariter αἰῶνα.
anchorLine: ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι αἰῶνι (l).
en: In the age to come. Chrysostom, in the Comparison of a King and a Monk, a little before the end: 'Concerning the affairs of the present life I think enough has been said; but if we should wish also to examine the coming contest...' One should read 'aiona' (accusative). The same author, or someone else, at the beginning of the indiction, vol. 5, Savile, p. 815, l. 23: 'We do not worship the contest that draws us to corruption.' Here too I want 'aiona'.

text: Τοῦ μὴ ἔχοντος ποῦ τὴν κεφαλὴν κλῖναι. Elegantissimus erit locus Palladii, si commode legatur. In Vita Chrysostomi, cap. 19 : Εἷς ἀνωφελής, καὶ ἀχρηστος, ὄχλος ἐστίν· οἷος ἦν ὁ εἰπὼν τῷ Ἰησοῦ· « Διδάσκαλε, ἀκολουθήσω σοι, ὅπου ἐὰν ἀπέρχῃ. » Οὗ φυγὼν τὸν ὄχλον ὁ Σωτὴρ εἶπεν τό· « Αἱ ἀλώπεκες, » καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. Hoc est : Unus inutilis, et agyrta, turba est : qualis erat is qui dixit Jesu : « Magister, sequar te, quocunque ieris. » Cujus fugiens turbam Servator, dixit illud : « Vulpes foveas habent ; » et reliqua. (Matth. viii, 20.)
anchorLine: Μνημονεύσωμεν τοῦ μὴ ἔχοντος ποῦ τὴν κεφαλὴν κλίνῃ (m).
en: 'Of him who had nowhere to lay his head.' The passage of Palladius will be most elegant if it is read properly. In the Life of Chrysostom, ch. 19: 'One useless and vagabond is a crowd: such was he who said to Jesus, "Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go." Fleeing his crowd the Saviour said, "The foxes..."' and so on. That is: one useless vagrant is a crowd; such was he who said to Jesus, 'Master, I will follow you wherever you go'; fleeing his crowd the Saviour said, 'Foxes have holes', etc. (Matt. 8:20.)
